lesson.title: The Full Swing: Bipolar I Disorder
lesson.summary: Bipolar I disorder is defined by the occurrence of at least one full manic episode, a criterion that sets it apart from every disorder built only on depression.
lesson.body:
Most mood disorders discussed so far involve depression without its opposite pole: mood drops, but it does not also swing up into a distinct high. Bipolar I disorder introduces that second pole. The single requirement for diagnosis is at least one manic episode, a distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood combined with sharply increased energy and activity, lasting at least a week or, if it is severe enough to require hospitalization, any length of time at all. Notably, a major depressive episode is not required for the diagnosis. In practice, however, the great majority of people with bipolar I disorder do experience depressive episodes as well, cycling between the two poles over the course of their lives, which is why the disorder is grouped conceptually near major depressive disorder even though its defining feature is mania rather than depression.

This is part of why the DSM classification system treats bipolar and related disorders as their own chapter, positioned between the depressive disorders and the disorders involving psychosis, rather than folding bipolar I simply into the depressive disorders category. It shares surface features with depression (the low periods can look identical to a major depressive episode) while also sharing features with disorders involving impaired reality testing, since severe mania can include psychotic symptoms like delusions or hallucinations. Applying the general framework for defining psychological disorders is useful here too: mania causes real dysfunction (impaired ability to work, parent, manage money, or stay safe), real distress (to the person or, often more so, to the people around them), and behavior that clearly deviates from that person's own baseline functioning, not just from social norms.

A well documented public example is the clinical psychologist Kay Redfield Jamison, who has written openly about living with bipolar I disorder, including periods of mania marked by racing thoughts, grandiosity, and reckless decisions, alternating with severe depressive episodes. Her account is useful precisely because it illustrates both poles in one person: the same individual who could be a competent, insightful researcher during stable periods experienced episodes where their mood, energy, and judgment became dramatically and dangerously different from their usual self. That contrast, between a person's stable baseline and a period of clearly abnormal functioning, is at the heart of how mania is recognized clinically, and the next chapter examines exactly what that manic episode involves in more detail.
